title: The five ratios
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define and calculate the gross profit margin, profit margin, return on capital employed, current ratio and acid test ratio, and interpret what each figure says about the business behind it.

blocks.heading: Gross profit margin
blocks.text: The gross profit margin measures trading performance: the share of revenue left after paying for the goods themselves. It is calculated as (gross profit divided by revenue) x 100, where gross profit is revenue less the cost of the goods sold. A margin of 40% means 40 cents of every Namibian dollar of sales remains after buying what was sold - the pool out of which every other cost must be paid. The figure earns its meaning in comparison: set against last year's margin and a rival's, it becomes evidence about whether the business is buying and selling better or worse than before.

blocks.heading: Gross profit margin worked out
blocks.text:
Ongelo Tailors of Windhoek had revenue of N$450 000 last year and cost of sales of N$270 000. Gross profit is 450 000 - 270 000 = 180 000 in Namibian dollars, so the margin is 180 000 divided by 450 000, which is 0.4, or 40%. The year before it was 34%.

Interpretation: the margin rose by 6 percentage points, which usually means the tailors sold at better prices or bought fabric more cheaply. Compared against the earlier year, each sale now leaves a larger share of revenue as gross profit - a wider pool from which rent, wages and ultimately profit itself must be paid.

blocks.heading: Profit margin
blocks.text: The profit margin measures the share of revenue left after every cost - the goods, wages, rent, marketing, everything - has been paid. It is calculated as (profit divided by revenue) x 100. Where the gross profit margin watches the buying and selling side, the profit margin watches the whole business, so it is usually the lower of the two figures. A margin of 8% means 8 cents of every Namibian dollar of sales remains after every cost - the share that is truly the owner's.

blocks.heading: Profit margin worked out
blocks.text:
Omaruru Hardware had revenue of N$600 000, gross profit of N$360 000 and operating expenses of N$150 000. Profit is 360 000 - 150 000 = 210 000 in Namibian dollars, so the profit margin is 210 000 divided by 600 000, which is 0.35, or 35%. Its gross profit margin is 360 000 divided by 600 000, which is 0.6, or 60%.

Interpretation: the 25-percentage-point gap between 60% and 35% shows how heavily expenses bear on the trade. The owner can lift the profit margin by selling at better prices, buying stock more cheaply, or trimming expenses such as rent and wages, because each route raises the share of revenue left as profit.

blocks.heading: Return on Capital Employed
blocks.text: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) measures how hard the long-term funds work: profit as a percentage of capital employed, calculated as (profit divided by capital employed) x 100. Capital employed here names the long-term funds invested in the business - the owner's equity plus any non-current liabilities. The word capital does three jobs in business studies, and the senses must be kept apart: money capital is money placed into the business, capital goods are machines and buildings, and capital employed is the ratio input used here.

blocks.heading: ROCE worked out
blocks.text:
Swakop Coastal Tours made a profit of N$84 000 on capital employed of N$600 000. ROCE is 84 000 divided by 600 000, which is 0.14, or 14%. A bank deposit in Windhoek might pay about 8% for the same period.

Interpretation: compared against that 8%, the tour company's 14% suggests its long-term funds are working productively - the owners are earning more from the business than the money would fetch in a savings account. Read the other way, a ROCE persistently below the interest rate suggests the funds might be better placed elsewhere, which is why the figure is usually set against interest rates and against what rival firms achieve.

blocks.heading: Current ratio
blocks.text: The current ratio is a liquidity measure: current assets divided by current liabilities, normally written in a form such as 2 to 1. Current assets are inventory, trade receivables and cash; current liabilities are the debts due within a year, such as amounts owed to suppliers and an overdraft. The figure says how many Namibian dollars of current assets stand behind each Namibian dollar of short-term debt.

blocks.heading: Current ratio worked out
blocks.text:
Walvis Bay Cold Storage holds current assets of N$132 000 - inventory N$60 000, receivables N$48 000, cash N$24 000 - and current liabilities of N$66 000. The current ratio is 132 000 divided by 66 000, which is 2, written 2 to 1: for each N$1 of short-term debt the business holds N$2 of current assets.

Interpretation: a figure below 1 would suggest difficulty paying debts as they fall due, while a very high figure, say 4, suggests cash and stock sitting idle instead of earning. Note that this 2 includes N$60 000 of inventory, the slowest asset to turn into cash - which is exactly why the acid test exists.

blocks.heading: Acid test ratio
blocks.text: The acid test ratio is the stricter liquidity measure: current assets less inventory, divided by current liabilities. It counts only the assets that can be turned into cash quickly - receivables and cash itself - because a payment due this month usually cannot wait for stock to be sold first.

blocks.heading: Acid test worked out
blocks.text:
Etosha Gate Lodge holds current assets of N$90 000, of which inventory is N$40 000, and current liabilities of N$50 000. Current assets less inventory are 90 000 - 40 000 = 50 000 in Namibian dollars, so the acid test is 50 000 divided by 50 000, which is 1, written 1 to 1. Its current ratio, for contrast, is 90 000 divided by 50 000, which is 1.8.

Interpretation: the lodge clears the current ratio comfortably but only just meets the acid test, because much of its wealth sits in stock. A result below 1 would suggest reliance on selling inventory to pay near-term debts, so a firm with slow-moving stock may need to delay purchases, negotiate longer credit or arrange an overdraft.

blocks.heading: Two confusions to keep apart
blocks.text: Two pairs are constantly swapped. Gross profit margin and profit margin differ in what they subtract: the first takes away only the cost of the goods sold, the second takes away every expense, so a strong gross margin can sit beside a loss. The test: ask which costs were taken out before the figure was reached. Current ratio and acid test differ in one input: the first counts inventory, the second removes it, so a business can pass one and fail the other. The test: ask whether stock is inside the figure, and whether that stock could become money before the next payment date.

blocks.heading: Reading a set of results
blocks.text:
Ratios earn their keep in sets. A tour operator in Queenstown, New Zealand, judging a supplier, might read a gross profit margin of 30% (weak trading), a profit margin of 4% (expenses swallow almost the whole trading profit), a ROCE of 3% (long-term funds earn little), a current ratio of 2.6 and an acid test of 1.9 (short-term debts comfortably covered). Judged on liquidity alone the supplier looks sound; judged on profitability the same business looks fragile. That is the point: profitability ratios and liquidity ratios answer different questions, and a business can be strong on one side and weak on the other.

Read the trend as well as the level - a margin that slips a little every year tells a different story from one dip in an otherwise rising line - and compare against firms in the same trade, because a 4% margin may be normal for a food retailer and thin for a jeweller. An investor choosing between businesses weighs the return figures; a lender weighing the same set looks first at the liquidity pair, so the same numbers feed different decisions.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Every figure these ratios use comes from the accounts of topics 5.3 and 5.4: revenue, gross profit and profit from the income statement; current assets, current liabilities and capital employed from the statement of financial position. Topic 5.2 forecasts the cash side, and 6.1 shows how results like these feed long-run decisions.
